title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Earlier safety settings cover harmful responses or text-based threats; our setting covers untrusted visual inputs that change an agent's intent and actions.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, ours highlighted with red border
description: Three side-by-side rounded panels with matching vertical structure: 1. Multimodal Safety, 2. Text Agent Safety, and 3. Multimodal Agent Safety. The third panel has a red border and red title. Each panel starts with a small input → model → output flow. The icons are image and document inputs, a brain model icon (with a wrench in panels 2 and 3), and text or API/terminal action outputs. A dashed line separates the flow from a target-icon 'Focus' line. Below that is an example threat. Panel 1 shows a bomb image with a harmful question. Panel 2 shows a hidden email instruction. Panel 3 shows an image with a harmful instruction and a fake 'System Authorization' dialog screenshot. Each panel has a red-highlighted outcome with a sad robot, then a yellow warning box reading Response-level or Action-level safety. The eye goes first to the red third panel.
caption: Comparison of multimodal-model safety, text-agent safety, and multimodal-agent safety. The first evaluates harmful responses, the second evaluates unsafe actions caused by text-based threats, and the third evaluates changes in both intent and action caused by untrusted visual observations.
abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.
